summary: Describes the NEA Asokan Attack, a subtle forwarding attack against Network Endpoint Assessment protocols, which check the health of devices joining a network. It explains how the attack works and what countermeasures can be used. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A sneaky person walks up to the door wearing a healthy friend's wristband instead of showing their own. This explains the trick and how guards can stop it.

how to protect network endpoint assessment from forwarding attacks
how to protect endpoint assessment from attacks
subtitle: A forwarding attack against endpoint health assessment protocols and countermeasures.

tldr.problem: Network Endpoint Assessment (NEA) protocols verify that devices joining a network are secure before granting access. An attacker can use a man-in-the-middle attack to forward health attestations from a clean device to a dirty (compromised) device, fooling the server into granting access to the attacker's infected machine.
tldr.mechanism: The attacker positions itself between a clean endpoint (or a trusted measurement device) and a compromised endpoint. It forwards the authentication exchange, causing the server to believe the posture claims originated from the compromised device.
tldr.outcome: This attack allows infected machines onto secure networks. Countermeasures include binding identities of tunnel endpoints into the protocol and cryptographic binding of the assessment exchange to the underlying transport layer using channel binding data.

today: RFC 6813 is an Informational RFC documenting a security vulnerability in NEA protocols. It has not been obsoleted. The PT-TLS and PT-EAP protocols incorporate the recommended cryptographic binding countermeasure to mitigate this attack.

sections.title: Network Endpoint Assessment and the Need for Posture Checking
sections.content:
Network Endpoint Assessment (NEA) protocols allow a network to check the security posture (health status) of devices before they join. The NEA Reference Model consists of nested protocols: Posture Attribute (PA) messages nested in Posture Broker (PB) protocol, all nested in a Posture Transport (PT) protocol.

The NEA Server evaluates claims about what software and security settings are present on the endpoint. If the device appears compromised (missing patches, disabled firewalls), the server can deny access or isolate the device. This is critical for protecting networks from infected machines.

The PT protocols (PT-TLS and PT-EAP) include mechanisms for cryptographic and identity binding to defend against the NEA Asokan Attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Before people enter a building, a guard checks their health. NEA is like that check, but for computers. The guard wants to make sure the computer is healthy (has updates, antivirus, etc.) before it joins the company network.

sections.title: How the NEA Asokan Attack Works
sections.content:
The NEA Asokan Attack is a variation of a 2002 attack by Asokan, Niemi, and Nyberg. In the original attack, an attacker tricks an authorized user into authenticating to a decoy server, which forwards the authentication protocol through another tunnel to trick the real server.

In the NEA variant, the attacker has three entities: a CleanEndpoint (a trusted device with good posture), a BadServer (an intermediate server under the attacker's control), and a DirtyEndpoint (the attacker's compromised machine). The attack flow is: CleanEndpoint sends posture claims (PA messages) to BadServer, which forwards them to DirtyEndpoint, which relays them to the GoodServer (the legitimate NEA server). GoodServer receives the claims and believes they came from DirtyEndpoint, not CleanEndpoint. It concludes that DirtyEndpoint is clean and grants access.
sections.plainLanguage: The attacker finds a healthy person and an unhealthy person. The attacker makes the unhealthy person wear the healthy person's health monitor while both go to the door. The guard thinks the unhealthy person is actually the healthy person and lets them in.

sections.title: Defending Against Lying Endpoints with External Measurement
sections.content:
One defense against simple endpoint lying is to use an External Measurement Agent (EMA): secure hardware, software, or firmware designed to accurately report endpoint configuration. An EMA observes critical posture aspects and sends integrity-protected claims directly to the NEA Server's Posture Validator.

The Posture Collector on the endpoint and intermediaries between the EMA and Posture Validator are untrusted; messages only carry integrity protection, replay protection, and source authentication between the EMA and Posture Validator. The EMA must obtain cryptographic binding data from the TLS exchange and prove knowledge of it in an exchange that provides integrity and replay protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of trusting what the computer says about itself, use a special secure device on the computer that cannot be fooled. That device sends the truth directly to the guard.

sections.title: Cryptographic Binding as a Countermeasure
sections.content:
The recommended defense is cryptographic binding: the PA exchange is bound to the PT exchange and to the keying material granted as a result. This ensures the NEA Server knows that the PA claims pertain to the same endpoint that terminated the PT exchange, and no third party gains access from this exchange.

The TLS handshake establishes cryptographic state. Two mechanisms extract binding data: Keying Material Exporters (RFC 5705) allow additional key material to be extracted from the TLS master secret. The tls-unique Channel Binding Data (RFC 5929) extracts data from the TLS handshake finished message. The RFC recommends the tls-unique approach, which works with any TLS cipher suite based on a strong cipher algorithm.

For robust binding, the TLS cipher suite must not allow a single party to control the pre-master secret. Diffie-Hellman-based cipher suites (such as RSA-DHE) meet this requirement; key-transport suites (such as RSA) do not.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard locks the health check to the specific person. The health check contains a secret code that only works with that person's ID and appearance. If someone else tries to use a stolen health check, the code does not match and the guard knows it is fake.
